[Level 4 · Models & learning]{.level-4} [⏱ ~90 min]{} [Prerequisites: [The ML workflow](44-ml-workflow.qmd), [Random forests](46-random-forests.qmd), [Gradient boosting](47-gradient-boosting.qmd), [SVMs](48-svm.qmd)]{}

::: {.callout-note .objectives}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- compare several models **fairly**, on the same resamples and with the same metrics, using `workflow_set()` and `workflow_map()`;
- read `autoplot()` and `rank_results()` output and judge whether differences are larger than their uncertainty;
- choose a model using **performance, simplicity, interpretability and calibration**, and draw a **calibration plot**;
- finalise the chosen workflow and evaluate it **exactly once** on the test set with `last_fit()`;
- compute **permutation importance** for any model, and list the main questions of responsible use.
:::

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source(here::here("_common.R"))
```

```{r}
#| label: packages
library(tidymodels)   # includes workflowsets
library(rpart)        # engine: decision tree
library(ranger)       # engine: random forest
library(xgboost)      # engine: boosted trees
library(kernlab)      # engine: SVM
```

## 1. Why compare models systematically?

In the last five lessons we fitted five kinds of model to the Titanic data. Which one should we use? It is tempting to look back at the numbers printed in each lesson and pick the largest. That would be a mistake for three reasons:

- **Different conditions.** If two models were evaluated with different folds, different metrics or different preprocessing, their numbers are not comparable.
- **Noise.** Cross-validated estimates have a standard error. A difference of 0.005 in AUC may be pure chance.
- **The test set.** Each lesson called `last_fit()` once — fine for teaching, but if we now choose the model with the best *test* score, the test set has become part of the selection, and its score is optimistic.

There is also no universally best method (this is sometimes called the *no free lunch* principle): which model works best depends on the data. The honest procedure is:

1. evaluate **all candidates on the same resamples of the training set**, with the same metrics;
2. choose one, using performance *and* other criteria;
3. only then, evaluate the chosen one **once** on the test set.

## 2. Data, split, folds and metrics

Exactly as in [the ML workflow lesson](44-ml-workflow.qmd):

```{r}
#| label: titanic-data
titanic <- readr::read_csv(data_path("titanic_data.csv"),
                           na = c("", "NA", "?"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(survived, pclass, sex, age, sibsp, parch, fare, embarked) |>
  mutate(
    survived = factor(survived, levels = c(1, 0), labels = c("yes", "no")),
    pclass   = factor(pclass, levels = 1:3, labels = c("1st", "2nd", "3rd")),
    sex      = factor(sex),
    embarked = factor(embarked)
  )

set.seed(2026)
titanic_split <- initial_split(titanic, prop = 0.75, strata = survived)
titanic_train <- training(titanic_split)
titanic_test  <- testing(titanic_split)
set.seed(2026)
titanic_folds <- vfold_cv(titanic_train, v = 5, strata = survived)
titanic_metrics <- metric_set(roc_auc, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity,
                              brier_class, mn_log_loss)
```

### Two recipes

Models differ in what preprocessing they need. Logistic regression, SVMs and XGBoost need numeric predictors (dummy variables); SVMs also need normalisation. Trees and forests work directly with factors.

```{r}
#| label: recipes
dummy_rec <- recipe(survived ~ ., data = titanic_train) |>
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_log(fare, offset = 1) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

basic_rec <- recipe(survived ~ ., data = titanic_train) |>
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors())
```

`dummy_rec` is the recipe of lesson 44; `basic_rec` the one used for trees and forests in lessons 45 and 46. Normalising is harmless for boosted trees, so they can share `dummy_rec`.

### Five model specifications

```{r}
#| label: specs
lr_spec <- logistic_reg() |>
  set_engine("glm")

tree_spec <- decision_tree(cost_complexity = tune(), tree_depth = tune(),
                           min_n = 10) |>
  set_engine("rpart")

rf_spec <- rand_forest(mtry = tune(), min_n = tune(), trees = 500) |>
  set_engine("ranger")

xgb_spec <- boost_tree(trees = tune(), tree_depth = tune(),
                       learn_rate = tune()) |>
  set_engine("xgboost")

svm_spec <- svm_rbf(cost = tune(), rbf_sigma = tune()) |>
  set_engine("kernlab")

all_specs <- list(lr_spec, tree_spec, rf_spec, xgb_spec, svm_spec)
all_specs <- lapply(all_specs, \(s) set_mode(s, "classification"))
names(all_specs) <- c("logistic", "tree", "forest", "boost", "svm")
```

The specifications are those of the previous lessons, slightly simplified (500 trees for the forest; for boosting we tune the number of trees directly instead of using early stopping).

## 3. A workflow set

A **workflow set** holds many workflows — combinations of a preprocessor and a model — in one table. `workflow_set(preproc, models)` crosses every preprocessor with every model; since our two recipes go with different models, we build two sets and stack them:

```{r}
#| label: workflow-set
dummy_set <- workflow_set(
  preproc = list(dummy = dummy_rec),
  models = all_specs[c("logistic", "boost", "svm")]
)
basic_set <- workflow_set(
  preproc = list(basic = basic_rec),
  models = all_specs[c("tree", "forest")]
)
all_wf <- bind_rows(dummy_set, basic_set)
all_wf
```

Each row has an identifier `wflow_id` made of the preprocessor and model names (`dummy_logistic`, `basic_forest`, …). The `result` column is still empty.

### Tune everything on the same folds

`workflow_map()` applies one tuning function to every workflow in the set:

```{r}
#| label: workflow-map
all_res <- all_wf |>
  workflow_map(
    "tune_grid",
    resamples = titanic_folds,
    grid = 10,
    metrics = titanic_metrics,
    seed = 123,
    control = control_grid(save_pred = TRUE, save_workflow = TRUE),
    verbose = TRUE
  )
all_res
```

- `grid = 10` asks `tune_grid()` to build a space-filling grid of 10 candidate combinations for each model. `mtry`, whose range depends on the number of predictors, is finalised automatically from the data.
- The logistic regression has no tuning parameters; `workflow_map()` then simply runs `fit_resamples()` for it.
- `seed = 123` sets the same random seed before each workflow, so the results are reproducible.
- `save_pred = TRUE` keeps the out-of-fold predictions (needed for the calibration plot); `save_workflow = TRUE` keeps the workflow inside the results.

In total about 4 × 10 × 5 + 5 = 205 models are fitted; on a laptop this takes a few minutes, mostly for the forests and the SVMs.

## 4. Reading the comparison

```{r}
#| label: fig-autoplot
#| fig-cap: "Cross-validated ROC AUC of the best configuration of each model, with error bars. Models are ranked from best (left) to worst."
autoplot(all_res, rank_metric = "roc_auc", metric = "roc_auc",
         select_best = TRUE) +
  geom_text(aes(y = mean - 0.02, label = wflow_id), angle = 90, hjust = 1) +
  expand_limits(y = 0.65) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

```{r}
#| label: rank-results
ranked <- rank_results(all_res, rank_metric = "roc_auc",
                       select_best = TRUE) |>
  filter(.metric %in% c("roc_auc", "brier_class")) |>
  select(wflow_id, .metric, mean, std_err, rank) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = .metric,
                     values_from = c(mean, std_err)) |>
  arrange(rank)
ranked
```

::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output

- `select_best = TRUE` keeps, for each workflow, only its **best** tuning configuration; `rank` orders the workflows by mean ROC AUC.
- The error bars in the plot (and `std_err` in the table) show the uncertainty of each estimate. Typically on these data the flexible models and the logistic regression are **within one or two standard errors** of each other; the single tree is often a little behind.
- Look at the Brier score as well: a model can rank passengers well (high AUC) but give less accurate probabilities (higher Brier).
- The best workflow here is `r ranked$wflow_id[1]` with a mean AUC of `r round(ranked$mean_roc_auc[1], 3)` (standard error `r round(ranked$std_err_roc_auc[1], 3)`).
:::

### Are the differences real?

Because all models used the **same folds**, we can compare them fold by fold: if one model beats another on every fold, that is more convincing than a difference of averages.

```{r}
#| label: fold-auc
fold_auc <- function(wflow) {
  res <- extract_workflow_set_result(all_res, wflow)
  best <- select_best(res, metric = "roc_auc")
  collect_metrics(res, summarize = FALSE) |>
    filter(.metric == "roc_auc", .config == best$.config) |>
    transmute(fold = id, wflow_id = wflow, auc = .estimate)
}
per_fold <- purrr::map(all_res$wflow_id, fold_auc) |>
  purrr::list_rbind() |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = wflow_id, values_from = auc)
per_fold
```

Each row is a fold, each column a model. If the columns go up and down **together**, the folds differ in difficulty and the models track each other; the differences between columns within a row are what matter. (A formal analysis of such paired results is possible, e.g. with the `tidyposterior` package; here we keep to the visual comparison.)

## 5. Choosing a model

Performance is only one criterion. Others matter just as much in practice:

| Criterion | Question | On the Titanic |
|---|---|---|
| **Performance** | Is it clearly better than the alternatives, beyond the noise? | Often differences of about one standard error |
| **Simplicity** | Fewer moving parts, easier to maintain and to reproduce? | Logistic < tree < forest < SVM ≈ boosting |
| **Interpretability** | Can we explain predictions to the people affected? | Logistic regression and a small tree can be read directly |
| **Calibration** | Do predicted probabilities match observed frequencies? | Check with a calibration plot (below) |
| **Cost** | Training and prediction time, memory, software dependencies | The SVM and the forest are the slowest here |

A sensible rule, analogous to the 1-SE rule of [the decision-tree lesson](45-decision-trees.qmd): **among the models whose AUC is within one standard error of the best, choose the simplest.**

```{r}
#| label: choose
simplicity <- c(dummy_logistic = 1, basic_tree = 2, basic_forest = 3,
                dummy_svm = 4, dummy_boost = 5)
best <- ranked |> slice_min(rank, n = 1)

candidates <- ranked |>
  filter(mean_roc_auc >= best$mean_roc_auc - best$std_err_roc_auc) |>
  mutate(simplicity = unname(simplicity[wflow_id])) |>
  arrange(simplicity)
candidates
chosen_id <- candidates$wflow_id[1]
chosen_id
```

With this rule the chosen workflow is **`r chosen_id`**. The ranking of "simplicity" is a judgement call, and you may disagree with ours; the important thing is to **decide the rule before looking at the test set**.

### Calibration

A model is **well calibrated** if, among the passengers to whom it gives a survival probability of about 0.7, about 70% actually survived. We check this with the out-of-fold predictions saved during tuning: group the predictions into bins, and compare the average predicted probability with the observed proportion of survivors in each bin.

```{r}
#| label: calibration-data
cv_preds <- collect_predictions(all_res, select_best = TRUE,
                                metric = "roc_auc")

calib <- cv_preds |>
  mutate(bin = cut(.pred_yes, breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.1),
                   include.lowest = TRUE)) |>
  summarise(predicted = mean(.pred_yes),
            observed = mean(survived == "yes"),
            n = n(),
            .by = c(wflow_id, bin))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-calibration
#| fig-cap: "Calibration of the five models (out-of-fold predictions, best configuration of each). Points on the diagonal mean that predicted probabilities match observed frequencies; point size is the number of passengers in the bin."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6
ggplot(calib, aes(predicted, observed)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(colour = "#0072B2") +
  geom_point(aes(size = n), colour = "#0072B2") +
  facet_wrap(~ wflow_id) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Mean predicted P(survival) in the bin",
       y = "Observed proportion of survivors", size = "Passengers")
```

```{r}
#| label: cv-brier
cv_preds |>
  group_by(wflow_id) |>
  brier_class(truth = survived, .pred_yes) |>
  arrange(.estimate)
```

::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output

- Points **below** the diagonal mean the model is **over-confident** in survival (it predicts, say, 0.8 where only 65% survived); points **above** it mean it is too pessimistic.
- Bins with few passengers (small points) are noisy; do not over-interpret them.
- Logistic regression, which estimates probabilities by maximum likelihood, tends to be reasonably calibrated. SVM probabilities come from Platt scaling ([lesson 48](48-svm.qmd)) and tree probabilities take only a few distinct values (one per leaf), which shows as a few large points.
- The Brier score summarises calibration and discrimination together; lower is better.
:::

If a model ranks well but is poorly calibrated, its probabilities can be recalibrated (the `probably` package provides tools for this), but the recalibration must itself be estimated on training data only.

## 6. The final test — exactly once

We now finalise the chosen workflow with its best tuning parameters, fit it on the whole training set and evaluate it on the test set:

```{r}
#| label: final-fit
chosen_params <- all_res |>
  extract_workflow_set_result(chosen_id) |>
  select_best(metric = "roc_auc")

final_wf <- all_res |>
  extract_workflow(chosen_id) |>
  finalize_workflow(chosen_params)

final_fit <- last_fit(final_wf, split = titanic_split,
                      metrics = titanic_metrics)
collect_metrics(final_fit)
```

```{r}
#| label: cv-vs-test
cv_auc <- ranked$mean_roc_auc[ranked$wflow_id == chosen_id]
test_auc <- collect_metrics(final_fit) |>
  filter(.metric == "roc_auc") |>
  pull(.estimate)
c(cv = cv_auc, test = test_auc)
```

The cross-validated AUC of the chosen model was `r round(cv_auc, 3)`; on the test set it is `r round(test_auc, 3)`. The two should be close (the test set has only `r nrow(titanic_test)` passengers, so a difference of a few hundredths is within the noise). This test value is what we report. If it were much worse, we would have learned something important — but we must **not** now go back, pick another model and test again: the test set would no longer be independent of our choices.

```{r}
#| label: fig-final-roc
#| fig-cap: "ROC curve of the chosen model on the test set."
collect_predictions(final_fit) |>
  roc_curve(truth = survived, .pred_yes) |>
  autoplot()
```

## 7. Explaining the chosen model: permutation importance

**Permutation importance** works for *any* model, because it only needs predictions: shuffle one predictor in a data set, predict again, and measure how much the performance drops. We compute it on the test set, for the original seven variables (not the dummy columns), using the fitted workflow so that the recipe is applied automatically.

```{r}
#| label: fig-perm-importance
#| fig-cap: "Permutation importance of the chosen model on the test set: decrease in ROC AUC when each variable is shuffled (20 repetitions)."
final_model <- extract_workflow(final_fit)

set.seed(2026)
perm_imp <- permutation_importance(
  final_model, data = titanic_test, outcome = "survived",
  prob_col = ".pred_yes", event_level = "first", nsim = 20
)

ggplot(perm_imp, aes(x = importance,
                     y = reorder(variable, importance, FUN = median))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "Decrease in ROC AUC when the variable is shuffled", y = NULL)
```

`permutation_importance()` is a short helper defined in the course file `_common.R` (open it: it is 20 lines of plain R). For each variable it shuffles the column, predicts again with the whole workflow and records how much the AUC drops.

- `prob_col = ".pred_yes"` is the predicted probability of survival, and `event_level = "first"` matches it: `"yes"` is the first level of `survived`, so the AUC is computed with survival as the event. A mismatch would give importance values with the wrong sign.
- `nsim = 20` repeats each shuffle 20 times; the boxes show how much the importance varies from one random permutation to another.
- The package `vip`, often used for this, was archived from CRAN in December 2025; the logic above is exactly what it computes.

Typically `sex` dominates, followed by `pclass` and `age`. As in [lesson 46](46-random-forests.qmd), remember that permutation importance describes **what the model uses**, not causal effects, and that correlated predictors (here `pclass` and `fare`) can share or mask each other's importance.

## 8. A note on responsible machine learning

A model that predicts well is not automatically a model that should be used. Before deploying a classifier, ask:

- **What is it for, and who is affected?** Predicting survival on the Titanic is a historical exercise. The same workflow applied to loans, hiring or medical triage makes decisions about people.
- **Which variables does it use?** Our model relies heavily on `sex`. That reflects a historical rule ("women and children first"), but in a modern application using a protected characteristic, or a proxy for it, may be unfair or illegal.
- **Does it work equally well for different groups?** Compute the metrics separately for relevant groups (e.g. `group_by(sex)` before `roc_auc()`); a good overall AUC can hide poor performance for a minority.
- **Will the future look like the training data?** Models degrade when the population changes (*data drift*). Monitor performance after deployment.
- **Are the probabilities trustworthy, and is the uncertainty communicated?** Report calibration and confidence in the estimates, not just a single accuracy figure.
- **Can it be reproduced and audited?** Keep the code, the seeds, the package versions and a short written description of data, intended use and limitations (sometimes called a *model card*).

::: {.callout-warning .pitfall}
## Common pitfalls

1. **Comparing models evaluated on different resamples or metrics.** Use one set of folds and one `metric_set()` for all candidates.
2. **Choosing the model with the best test score.** The test set is for the final report only; choose on CV results.
3. **Treating the top of `rank_results()` as a clear winner.** Check the standard errors; differences of about one standard error are not convincing.
4. **Ignoring calibration.** A high AUC says nothing about whether probabilities are accurate; use the Brier score and a calibration plot.
5. **Wrong event level in permutation importance or metrics.** The `pred_wrapper` probability and `event_level` must refer to the same class.
6. **Reading importance as causation**, or deploying a model without asking who is affected and how.
:::

## 9. Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q1. Why must all models be evaluated on the same folds?

So that differences in their scores are due to the models, not to the luck of different splits. Same folds also allow paired, fold-by-fold comparisons, which are more sensitive.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q2. Model A has CV AUC 0.862 (SE 0.012), model B 0.855 (SE 0.011). A is a boosted model, B a logistic regression. Which would you choose, and why?

The difference (0.007) is smaller than one standard error, so the data do not clearly favour A. B is simpler, faster, easier to explain and usually well calibrated, so B is a reasonable choice — unless calibration or other criteria favour A.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q3. In a calibration plot, the points for high predicted probabilities lie below the diagonal. What does that mean?

The model is **over-confident** for those passengers: it predicts high survival probabilities, but the observed proportion of survivors in those bins is lower.
:::

## 10. Exercises

::: {.exercise}
[★]{.stars} **Exercise 1 — a different metric.** Re-rank the workflows using the Brier score instead of ROC AUC (`rank_results(all_res, rank_metric = "brier_class", select_best = TRUE)`). Does the ranking change? Why can it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
rank_results(all_res, rank_metric = "brier_class", select_best = TRUE) |>
  filter(.metric == "brier_class") |>
  select(wflow_id, mean, std_err, rank)
```
For the Brier score smaller is better, and `rank_results()` takes this into account. The ranking can change because AUC measures only how well the model **ranks** passengers, while the Brier score also rewards **accurate probabilities**: a well-ranking but poorly calibrated model (e.g. the SVM, or a tree with few distinct probabilities) can move down.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 2 — add a sixth model.** Add a penalised logistic regression, `logistic_reg(penalty = tune(), mixture = 1) |> set_engine("glmnet")`, to the set with `dummy_rec` (see [lesson 43](../09-regression/43-penalized-regression.qmd)), and rerun the comparison. Does the lasso improve on ordinary logistic regression?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
lasso_spec <- logistic_reg(penalty = tune(), mixture = 1) |>
  set_engine("glmnet")
lasso_set <- workflow_set(preproc = list(dummy = dummy_rec),
                          models = list(lasso = lasso_spec))
lasso_res <- lasso_set |>
  workflow_map("tune_grid", resamples = titanic_folds, grid = 10,
               metrics = titanic_metrics, seed = 123)
bind_rows(all_res, lasso_res) |>
  rank_results(rank_metric = "roc_auc", select_best = TRUE) |>
  filter(.metric == "roc_auc") |>
  select(wflow_id, mean, std_err, rank)
```
With only about ten dummy-coded predictors and around a thousand training passengers, there is little to gain from shrinkage: the lasso is usually within a small fraction of a standard error of ordinary logistic regression. Penalisation helps most when there are many predictors relative to the number of observations. (`glmnet` must be installed.)
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 3 — interpret a calibration table.** For one model, the calibration bins give: predicted 0.15 / observed 0.10; predicted 0.45 / observed 0.47; predicted 0.85 / observed 0.70 (60 passengers in the last bin). Describe the model's calibration in two sentences. What would you check before drawing conclusions?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
The model is well calibrated in the middle range, slightly overestimates survival at low probabilities (it predicts 15% where 10% survived), and over-confident at the top: passengers given about 85% survival survived only 70% of the time. Before concluding, check the number of passengers in each bin and the uncertainty: with 60 passengers the observed proportion 0.70 has a standard error of about $\sqrt{0.7 \cdot 0.3 / 60} \approx 0.06$, so the gap of 0.15 is about 2.5 standard errors — suggestive, not conclusive.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 4 — debug the procedure.** A colleague tunes the five models with CV, then runs `last_fit()` on all five, and reports the model with the highest test AUC, together with that AUC, as "the expected performance on new passengers". What is wrong, and what should they do instead?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
The test set has been used to **select** the model, so the reported AUC is the maximum of five noisy estimates and is optimistic (a winner's-curse effect). They should choose the model on the cross-validated results of the training set (performance plus the other criteria), then run `last_fit()` **only for the chosen model** and report that single test score.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★★]{.stars} **Exercise 5 — performance by group.** Using `collect_predictions(final_fit)`, compute the ROC AUC, sensitivity and specificity of the final model separately for men and women (hint: the predictions do not contain `sex`; join them with the test set by row using `.row`, or use `augment(final_fit)`). What do you find, and why does it matter?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
test_pred <- augment(final_fit)          # test set + predictions
group_metrics <- metric_set(roc_auc, sensitivity, specificity)
test_pred |>
  group_by(sex) |>
  group_metrics(truth = survived, estimate = .pred_class, .pred_yes)
```
Within each sex the AUC is lower than overall, because much of the overall discrimination comes from separating women from men; within a group the model must rely on class and age. Sensitivity and specificity typically differ a lot between groups: the model predicts survival for most women and death for most men, so sensitivity is high for women and very low for men. In a real application such differences in error rates between groups would need to be reported and discussed.
:::
:::

## Summary

| Idea / function | What it does |
|---|---|
| `workflow_set(preproc, models)` | All combinations of preprocessors and models; stack sets with `bind_rows()` |
| `workflow_map("tune_grid", resamples, grid, metrics, seed)` | Tune every workflow on the same resamples |
| `autoplot(res, rank_metric, metric, select_best = TRUE)` | Compare the best configuration of each model |
| `rank_results(res, rank_metric, select_best = TRUE)` | Ranked table with means and standard errors |
| `collect_predictions(res, select_best = TRUE, metric)` | Out-of-fold predictions, e.g. for calibration |
| `extract_workflow_set_result()`, `extract_workflow()` | Retrieve one workflow's results / workflow |
| `select_best()`, `finalize_workflow()`, `last_fit()` | Fix parameters, refit on training, test once |
| `permutation_importance(wf, data, outcome, prob_col)` (course helper) | Model-agnostic permutation importance |

- Compare models on the **same resamples** with the **same metrics**; look at standard errors before declaring a winner.
- Choose by **performance, simplicity, interpretability, calibration and cost** — and fix the rule before looking at the test set.
- Use the test set **once**, for the chosen model only.
- Explain the model (permutation importance) and ask who is affected before using it.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
